entries.title: Serbia's Student List runs chemistry professor Radomir Saicic for president
entries.summary: After ousting strongman Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's student movement has now nominated academic Radomir Saicic for the upcoming presidential vote. Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of trying to collapse the state.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia's Student List runs chemistry professor for president

November 27, 2026

After ousting strongman Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's student movement has now nominated academic Radomir Saicic for the upcoming presidential vote. Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of trying to collapse the state.

A long-time supporter of the Serbian student movement, chemistry professor and researcher Radomir Saicic, is set to run for president on behalf of the Student List in late December.

Saicic accepted the nomination on Friday, a day after Serbia's new parliament scheduled the ballot for December 27.

In his acceptance speech, the Belgrade University lecturer said state institutions, including its president, needed to "win back public trust."

"It's time to restore dignity to the office of Serbian president," he said.

"Once we can agree with each other about things that matter to all of us despite our differences, Serbia will have the strength to decide its future on its own, and to have its voice heard and respected in the world," he added.

Vucic barred from running again

The 65-year-old is one of the lawmakers in the new assembly, which was formed in the wake of the Student List ousting the regime of Serbia's longtime strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic at the parliamentary polls last month.

Vucic is banned by the constitution from running for president after winning two terms. He has hinted at his party boycotting the presidential vote.

While the office of the Serbian president is officially far less powerful that the office of Serbian prime minister, Vucic managed to organize his rule around himself during his time as prime minister and then hold on to levers of power while serving as president.

Saicic sees Kosovo as 'occupied territory'

On Friday, Saicic accused the "outgoing regime" of "still trying to collapse our state."

"This past decade was marred by the breakdown of the rule of law, corruption, and hate speech," he said.

Saicic, a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Art, is seen by many as a moderate nationalist and a traditionalist.

He has notably described the neigboring, Albanian-dominated Kosovo, as "temporarily occupied territory," keeping in line with Belgrade's long-running policy of treating Kosovo as a breakaway province.

The presidential candidate has also urged a "productive relationship" with Russia, pointing to Serbia's energy needs.

Saicic pledges humility with Bible quote

While seemingly reticent on the topic of the European Union, Saicic told reporters on Friday that he has a "fundamentally positive stance toward Europe and European values," pointing to examples including environment protection, academic education, the rule of law, science and technological progress.

"All of these things we should develop as much as possible, not for the sake of meeting some formal criteria, but to actually be what we are supposed to be," he said.

Saicic has sought to present himself as a devout Orthodox Christian while simultaneously criticizing the Serbian church leaders for aligning with the Vucic regime.

In his Friday speech, Saicic quoted the Bible, saying that "whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant."

entries.title: Dutch authorities seize 26 critically endangered turtles from luggage of passenger bound for Hong Kong
entries.summary: The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport. 

The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico. They were only formally discovered and catalogued in 2018 and are one of the smallest of all known genuses of turtle.

"These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.

How were the turtles discovered and smuggled?

Dutch customs agents discovered the animals on November 21 during a regular inspection and then alerted the NVWA, as the responsible agency for such cases, on realizing that they had uncovered live fauna.

Police then arrested the man at the NVWA's request, and the NVWA said in Friday's statement that he was still in custody, with federal prosecutors continuing their investigations.

"Most of the turtles were packed in a box alongside a toy car, while others were placed inside a sealed sock within a suitcase," the NVWA wrote. "The animals had been wrapped in duct tape, which prevented them from moving. All of the turtles survived the journey."

Authorities said the turtles were being housed at a specialized rescue facility, "where the duct tape was carefully removed," and where they were "receiving the care they require."

What are Vallarta mud turtles?

Vallarta mud turtles are exceptionally small freshwater turtles that only entered the taxonomical record in 2018, endemic to a very small area in western Mexico.

Relatively little is known about the creature owing both to its recent discovery and the damage to its habitat caused by urbanization and a growing tourist trade in the Mexican state of Jalisco.

The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria — which recently started breeding the turtles in Austria as a "genetic reservoir for eventual rewilding" and is working to help preserve them in Mexico — considers it "the world's smallest turtle species," and estimates that "over 99%" of its natural habitat has been lost to urbanization.

Roads and traffic are a particular risk for the slow-moving creatures.

"Despite strict protections, their small size and striking appearance make them prime targets for illegal collectors," Turtle Island says when detailing other risks to the tiny animals, that are not known to grow larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.

The IUCN Red List classifies it as "Critically Endangered" and it is subject to the highest level of protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). 

"The suspected poaching of 26 of these turtles from the wild may have reduced the population by nearly 10%," the NVWA wrote, basing its figure on the estimated population of around 300 of the turtles in the wild.

The agency urged people to report any suspected instances of illegal trade of protected animal or plant species, whether "via online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets."

entries.title: Arsenic in the water: Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution
entries.summary: Thailand is seeking to tackle river pollution stemming from rare earth mines in neighboring Myanmar. The two countries held joint talks this week as a "first step towards agreeing on the evidence."
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

Thailand is seeking to tackle river pollution stemming from rare earth mines in neighboring Myanmar. The two countries held joint talks this week as a "first step towards agreeing on the evidence."

Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.

A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.

The reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup. 

The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.

Two sides agreed to joint water sampling

Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.

The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This will cover 12 water sampling locations and is expected to begin between December and January.

But no public agreement was made about Thailand's request for a six-month suspension of mining operations.

The talks follow the suspension of tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district earlier this month, near the Myanmar border, after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times higher than government limits.

Bangkok is also seeking China's help in pressuring private Chinese operators, given its position as the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, as the issue grows increasingly urgent after months of concern.

Authorities this week urged residents to avoid eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests detected dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in northern and northeastern Thailand.

Myanmar intervention to stop mining faces obstacles

"Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Thai Deputy ​Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said at the joint talks.

However, finding a solution remains a challenge.

Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), told AFP, "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity.”

But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult," he added.

Several ethnic armed groups have been active in the region for decades, while the civil war is still ongoing.

Thai authorities point to two gold mines across the border from Mae Sai as the main contributors to elevated arsenic levels in the Sai River.

The broader region is divided among various groups, including Myanmar's military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group closely aligned with China.

The main mining belts are currently outside the control of Myanmar's military-backed government, including sites in Shan State.

Thailand might ask China's help, PM says

Thai authorities are also seeking to assess whether pollutant mines are under the control of Myanmar's government or other entities, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan told Reuters.

"We also would like them to check whether they can control every mine or they cannot. If they cannot, we will ask China to help,” he said.

A spokesperson from China's foreign ministry told AFP that Beijing "pays close attention" to the pollution issue and would provide technical support.

entries.title: Georgia: Police clash with Besiktas fans at Israel club game
entries.summary: Turkey's Besiktas accused Georgian police of using "disproportionate" force during the game with Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva, which saw Besiktas fans unfurl a banner supporting Palestine.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

Turkey's Besiktas accused Georgian police of using "disproportionate" force during the game with Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva, which saw Besiktas fans unfurl a banner supporting Palestine.

A football game between a Turkish and an Israeli team in Georgia's Batumi was disrupted by violence, with UEFA due to assess the events on Friday.

Georgian police said 16 people were detained and three officers "sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions" during the match.

The police also accused some supporters of hurling stadium seats at security forces.

Turkey's Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were originally set to meet in Istanbul, but with the tensions between the two countries running high due to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, UEFA decided to move the match to Georgia for safety reasons.

Georgia denies police were deployed over Palestine support

During the Thursday game, Besiktas fans unfurled a banner, "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine," waved Palestinian flags and chanted anti-Israel slogans.

However, Georgian authorities insisted they did not intervene due to the fans expressing their support for the Palestinians.

"We categorically deny these reports and emphasize that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," said the Georgian Interior Ministry.

In turn, Besiktas accused the authorities of using "disproportionate force" against the fans, and Turkey's football federation condemned "the unacceptable attitudes, behavior and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium."

A Besiktas club employee told the AFP news agency that five Turkish fans were taken to a hospital for medical treatment.

The match was suspended for over half an hour due to the violence in the stands. Eventually, Danish referee Morten Krogh continued the game, which ended with Besiktas winning 2 to 1.

The Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Turkish government ministers close ranks with Besiktas

The unrest has prompted a diplomatic incident between Turkey and Georgia.

Turkish sources indicated Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the clashes with his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili.

Meanwhile, Turkish Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak and Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci echoed Besiktas' accusations of "disproportionate" force used by the Georgian police.

In an online post, Bak pledged to continue "resolutely defend the rights of Turkish sport and our fans."

Turkish news agency IHA reported that the 16 detained Besiktas fans have been released due to diplomatic and legal steps ordered by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

According to Besiktas, Erdogan also spoke to the club chairman, telling the sports official he was closely monitoring the situation.

entries.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
entries.summary: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East. 

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran. 

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf. 

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed. 

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

entries.title: German lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
entries.summary: German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Parliament approves €556 billion 2027 budget

Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026

German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German lawmakers to vote on 2027 federal budget
  • Left Party hosts summit on femicide and violence against women
  • BSW party conference starts in Dresden
  • Rheinmetall lowers revenue forecasts
  • Chancellor Merz to meet Pope Leo on Monday

Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.

Skip next section German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans

German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans

German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63."

At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.

In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.

From 2029 onwards, however, only periods of employment, child-rearing, and the care of relatives will count toward the 45-year contribution requirement.

Periods during which an insured person received unemployment benefits, sickness benefits or transitional allowances – or held only a low-wage, part-time "mini-job" – will no longer be credited.

For weeks, Germany's coalition government partners, the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and Schweitzer's center-left Social Democrats have been struggling to reach a compromise on this issue.

A pension commission had proposed abolishing this popular type of pension, a proposal opposed by the SPD.

A group of leading coalition politicians, including Schweitzer, reportedly held final discussions regarding the plans as recently as Wednesday evening.

Skip next section German parliament approves 2027 budget

German parliament approves 2027 budget

Germany's ‌lower ⁠house ⁠of parliament, the Bundestag, ​voted in favor of ​a €556 ​billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost ​defense ​and infrastructure spending.

Total new borrowing will reach €210 ​billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in ​2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild ​its military after decades of underinvestment.

"It is right that we invest in the railways and ​in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday, defending his budget. "It is right... that we invest in our security."

German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.

"We are putting up the ⁠money for ​defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil said. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again."

But there was criticism of the budget from the opposition Left Party, with party leader Ines Schwerdtner accusing the government only ever talking about emergency and war.

"But for millions of people in this country, the emergency comes every month when money gets tight," she said. "But you're not interested in these emergencies."

317 members of parliament voted in favor of the budget and 260 against it. There were no abstentions.

Skip next section Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo

Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will have a private audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Monday before meeting Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome later, a government spokesman confirmed on Friday.

Merz, himself a Catholic, had a brief encounter with Pope Leo at the pontiff's inauguration in May 2025, but this will be the pair's first private meeting.

According to Politico, who first reported on the planned meeting earlier this week, officials expect the discussion to focus on "human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine."

Afterwards, Merz will be received with military honors by Italian Prime Minister Meloni, with whom he will hold talks on Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, economic cooperation and, "with certainty," the European Union budget for the period 2028-2034, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF).

Negotiations over the MFF in Brussels this week ended without agreement, with Germany leading a group of more fiscally conservative member states which also includes Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Italy, on the other hand, along with countries like Poland and Spain, would like to see a more ambitious EU budget.

Skip next section Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast

Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast

German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has revised its medium-term revenue forecast for 2030 down from around €45 billion to between €33 billion and €37 billion, with an expected profit margin of around 20%.

The announcement, made on Friday at a market event in Hamburg, comes after the Düsseldorf-based company also lowered its forecast for the current year following delays in major orders  notably from the German government.

In July, the German defense ministry canceled a multi-billion-euro contract to produce six new type-F126 naval frigates and there are now reportedly delays in an expected large-scale order of Boxer armored fighting vehicles (AFV).

Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger said the government was negotiating hard on price and that he would only sign off on the deal once "sufficient profitability" was guaranteed.

Meanwhile, Rheinmetall is set to deliver 66 additional Lynx AFVs to Romania, part of an order which now totals 298 such vehicles.

The deliveries to the European Union and NATO member state are set to begin in 2028 and be completed by 2030.

Rheinmetall is also manufacturing four battleships for the Romanian navy and has increased its production capacities in the eastern European country which borders Ukraine.

Skip next section Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack

Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack

German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has confirmed that two of its employees had been killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.

"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, providing technical support for air-defense systems," the Düsseldorf-based company said in a statement.

"Protecting the people of that country was a matter of deep personal importance to them. Both the company's leadership and the entire workforce are devastated by the loss of our colleagues. We share in the grief of those they have left behind."

The two victims were Italian citizens who worked as technicians for subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirmed in Rome.

Tajani said the pair had been at an air surveillance station in Kuwait when it was attacked by two Iranian drones. Two other people, a Pakistani national and Kuwaiti army captain, were also injured.

The Iranian foreign ministry has denied any involvement in the deadly attack.

Rheinmetall secured a contract to supply the Kuwaiti navy with defense systems in July.

Skip next section BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference

BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference

Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.

The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.

After initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

BSW split over stance on AfD

Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — with which it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.

Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain issues which an AfD minority government would want to implement.

The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.

The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy."

"We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but said: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media."

Wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority."

But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.

"Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term."

They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier."

Skip next section Left Party hosts international femicide summit

Left Party hosts international femicide summit

Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is on Friday hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

Under the title "Voices Against Femicide," the summit in Berlin brings together activists, politicians and researchers from around the world, including Kenya, Nigeria, Kurdistan, India, Afghanistan, Syria, Mexico, Argentina, Spain and Germany.

Across three panel discussions, the speakers will highlight women's rights, feminist struggles and legal perspectives and debate political measures which are urgently needed in Germany to effectively combat femicides and patriarchal violence.

The summit comes just two days after Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, marked Orange Day, the United Nations' officially named day for the elimination of violence against women, with a minute's silence and a series of speeches.

Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office reported a total of 1,176 female victims of attempted and completed homicide in 2025, up from 859 in 2024.

The number of female victims of domestic violence in Germany in 2025 rose by 2.8% to 197,667.

Skip next section German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027

German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027

German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.

The plans call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germanyis talking about on Friday, 27 November.

The German parliament, the Bundestag, is set to vote on a 2027 federal budget that foresees around €556 billion ($610 billion) in spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.

Also in Berlin, Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.

Meanwhile, the left-wing populist BSW party is holding its party convention in Dresden as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats.

entries.title: As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
entries.summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.
entries.content:
The Gambia

As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?

November 27, 2026

President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.

Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.

President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and four other candidates.

The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.

What matters to voters

Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.

A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.

"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."

Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.

Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.

"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.

Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.

"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.

"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.

Jobs, cost of living top of mind

Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.

The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.

The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.

The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.

Alhagie Sama, a voter in Banjul, said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.

"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.

Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.

"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.

"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."

Election under observation

The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.

The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.

International observers are also monitoring the process.

Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.

The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.

"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.

Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."

The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

DW correspondent Aminata Sanyang in Gambia contributed reporting.

entries.title: On the arrest of Informer TV owner and editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
entries.summary: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable or whether this is another political power struggle.
entries.content:
Serbia

Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?

November 27, 2026

The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable or whether this is another political power struggle.

"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June last year.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by the police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching" and he labelled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.

The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures" and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted political opponents of the previous government, activists and independent journalists.

Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?

Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."

Court cases and compensation

The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.

Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.

According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.

Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).

Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.

Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.

SNS lawmakers protest

Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.

The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.

"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.

A reckoning or an internal power struggle?

Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.

The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

entries.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
entries.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.
entries.content:
Philippines

Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?

November 27, 2026

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.

"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

entries.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
entries.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.
entries.content:
November 27, 2026

War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW. 

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026. 

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.
